Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large training demands and memory needs. Brain structures, such as the cerebral cortex, operate in parallel, processing local information through connections, which raises the question of whether similar principles could improve neural networks by reducing their complexity. To investigate this, we developed Locality Masked RNNs (LM-RNNs) by incorporating a modulated, parallel processing mechanism into traditional RNNs. These networks comprise modules with internal connections that mimic brain cell connections within a region, allowing information to be exchanged among them through controlled gates. Performance tests using a memory game revealed that LM-RNNs consistently outperformed standard RNNs when working memory capacity was limited. Notably, under low memory conditions, LM-RNNs achieved comparable levels of accuracy to those provided by large, deeply-trained RNNs with ample memory. Additionally, we observed that LM-RNNs developed effective strategies, such as using the network's module structure to store and recall information, which often mirrored the approaches employed by successful RNNs with limited work memories. These results indicate that local, parallel mechanisms enhance the learning efficiency and data usage of RNNs, suggesting a more biologically plausible model for neural networks. This study's findings also provide insights into the types of problem solutions that are facilitated by these mechanisms, as well as the strategies used by RNNs. Based on these discoveries, we propose a new hypothesis claiming a fundamental relationship between the brain's parallel processing mechanisms and the capacity of neural networks to efficiently learn new information. This hypothesis could provide a framework for understanding this connection. To verify our hypothesis, we conducted additional experiments, which further validated it by demonstrating a correlation between the cognitive capabilities of the models and the biological plausibility of their architectures. This validation enabled us to identify six key factors contributing to the models' performance. Our study's findings demonstrate that complex problem solutions can be attributed not just to the memory, but also to the error correction and selection mechanisms. We also analyzed how these mechanisms interact with each other in various contexts. Furthermore, we investigated the connection between the brain's processing mechanisms and the capacity of neural networks to learn new information effectively. A new, biologically-inspired deep learning framework called LM-RNNs has been developed, which employs local, parallel processing mechanisms to enhance learning efficiency and data usage. We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, we examine anticommutative algebras of dimension n+1 and demonstrate a one-to-one correspondence between these and a specific subspace of the Grassmannian of n-dimensional anticommutative algebras. This discovery leads to a deeper understanding of the geometry involved, including divisors on these spaces, which in turn enables us to identify the cohomology rings of commutative and anticommutative algebras for any dimension n. Our work also provides explicit formulas for the Euler characteristic of each space, ultimately allowing us to compute the cohomology rings of nilpotent algebras for low dimensions. Furthermore, we identify isomorphisms between these algebras and specific Lie algebras based on their anticommutative properties. These findings expand on existing research in this field and offer novel insights into nilpotent algebras. Lastly, we include a list of open questions and areas for further investigation.

We've analyzed the data from a unique binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, based on our comprehensive photometry observations taken over 318 days. In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. By framing global pooling as an organized displacement of data points to a finite set of markers, the theory allows for an extensive exploration of pooling performances. The analysis demonstrates that the traditional global pooling module essentially resembles an one-to-one mapping from the data to the marker set, including the common average pooling, which is analytically equivalent to a specific transport plan. The study also proposes a computational approach to globally optimize pooling processes, offering a fundamental enhancement to the conventional empirical risk minimization used in deep learning. Additionally, the framework provides insights into the effectiveness of global pooling operations in neural networks and allows for the development of novel and efficient global pooling methods that surpass conventional implementations. The proposed framework and methods are thoroughly evaluated on standard datasets and show promising performance in binary classification tasks. The code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/lyzhi2016/GP_TPF. Furthermore, the theoretical framework has been incorporated into the PyTorch implementation as the Transport Pooling layer, which can be accessed through the PyTOCH repository at https://github.com/lyzhi2016/PyTOCH. The code for the deep learning experiments can be found at https://github.com/Chen-Ethan/Transport-Pooling-for-Deep-Learning. Ethan Chen contributed equally to this study. The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus (AGN) relation theory. We achieved this by gathering data on a diverse range of elliptical galaxies, incorporating spectroscopic information from the Gemini Multi-Object Demography from their nearest neighbor. We discovered 15 closest pairs and extracted their data from 91 elliptical galaxies within a specific luminosity range. We found that 11 out of 15 neighbor galaxies exhibited hot or warm emission, but only 4 had emission lines strong enough to indicate X-ray emission. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that 9 Seyfert type 1 elliptical galaxies primarily consist of spiral or lenticular galaxies. This suggests that 9 or 0 (depending on how you interpret the data) AGNs in our sample support the AGN relation theory, but 11 do not. We consider the validity of the AGN relation theory to be uncertain due to sampling issues and the need for further investigation. This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on flat general rotation surfaces characterized by a 1-type Gauss map. Additionally, it's established that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with this distinct Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if it's a Clifford torus. Furthermore, the paper classifies these surfaces based on their type-1 and type-2 Gauss maps being identically zero, revealing that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with a type-1 Gauss map being identically zero is a Lie group if and only if it's a product surface of a plane and a sphere. Using numerical examples, the paper demonstrates that a general rotation surface can be a Lie group when its type-2 Gauss map is identically zero, but this condition is insufficient for a non-planar, flat general rotation surface to be a Lie group when its type-1 Gauss map is identically zero. Lastly, the paper illustrates that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with a type-1 Gauss map being identically zero but a type-2 Gauss map not being identically zero is not a Lie group, whereas a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with a type-2 Gauss map being identically zero but a type-1 Gauss map not being identically zero is also a Lie group, exemplified by a Clifford torus. These findings complement and extend previous research on general rotational surfaces with a distinct Gauss map in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, including results by S. Azad and M. Azad, which involved classifying these surfaces based on their type-1 and type-2 Gauss maps being identically zero, with additional constraints. This research builds upon a body of work by S. Azad, M. Azad, K. Arslan, and Y. Yoon, who investigated type-1 and type-2 reversible general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, the study makes significant contributions to the area of differential geometry, extending prior research by S. Azad, M. Azad, A. U. Çelik, and Y. Yoon on general rotational surfaces with a distinct 1-type Gauss map in the 4-dimensional Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical spaces. further refining it using the collected data. Among the various methods employed,
many researchers believe that learning representations from video data can be
beneficial due to its abundance. Nevertheless, directly utilizing video data is
not always effective because it contains additional information (e.g. time) that
needs to be disregarded. In our research, we explored the potential of video
depth estimation as a pre-training method for semantic segmentation. By doing so,

complicating the pre-training task. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that
leveraging depth data from unlabeled videos is a viable option for

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is highly valuable in fields like sales, trading, and clinical analytics. Currently, narrative generation techniques such as language modeling and prompt engineering have limitations in providing specific insights about time-series trends and patterns. To address this, we present TCube, a neural framework for time-series narration that utilizes adaptive knowledge distillation to incorporate external expert knowledge derived from techniques like trend analysis, correlation mining, and spike detection. This allows TCube to generate more accurate, interpretable stories in less time compared to previous methods, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on multiple time-series datasets. This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora. Furthermore, this study sheds empirical light on the importance of pre-trained word embeddings in Japanese word segmentation. Specifically, the results show that vectors derived from the Vector Space Model (VSM) contribute substantially to the model's performance. Additionally, an optimal threshold for F1-score is identified for Japanese word segmentation. Lastly, this study explores the underlying mechanisms of LSTM for Japanese word segmentation using comprehensive annotation-based analysis and widespread agreement in prediction tasks. These findings provide valuable insights for developing Japanese word segmentation models. Nevertheless, the efficacy of these models is constrained when applied to texts lacking word annotations. As such, this study also ventures into the realm of semi-supervised learning for Japanese word segmentation. Specifically, the results indicate that models trained on datasets with few annotated words exhibit minimal declines in F1-score compared to models trained on fully annotated datasets. These findings have profound implications for developing data annotation strategies, particularly for large-scale datasets like Wikipedia. A thorough empirical analysis underpins this dissertation which culminates in a theoretical framework for Japanese word segmentation. Additionally, the source code and experimental data are publicly available for reproduction and further advancement of this research. Moreover, the Google Cloud platform facilitates the deployment of the Japanese word segmentation model for seamless integration into practical applications. On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities, where 82.5% of all links are external and 57.0% consist of frequently shared resources. To streamline users' knowledge management, this study delves into the characteristics of these shared links to identify common patterns in external resources that are repeatedly disseminated. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow, where analysis reveals that links to text-based documentation, tutorials, and other reference materials are most often reshared. This leads to observations such as users contributing identical knowledge across multiple posts, users reusing links for promotional purposes, and the issue of links referencing overwhelming amounts of data that can make information retrieval difficult. Our findings offer actionable insights to Stack Overflow moderators and researchers, including the recommendation to implement a centralized knowledge management system for maintaining and updating shared resources to preserve the integrity of the community's collaborative knowledge base. Furthermore, our study's conclusions can inform other Q\&A platforms dealing with similar issues to effectively leverage their collective knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose a research agenda consisting of three distinct approaches: gathering comprehensive statistics, implementing effective moderation, and developing innovative features to enhance the overall experience. This vision for the future acknowledges the inherent complexities of collaborative knowledge sharing and highlights the significance of addressing associated problems to realize the full potential of Q\&A platforms. Based on our analysis, we estimate that a significant portion of time spent by moderators could be devoted to implementing tailored strategies to maintain their unique characteristics. We provide empirical evidence to support this claim, underscoring the value of in-depth qualitative studies in informing design decisions for Q\&A platforms. We envision that the resulting theory-driven design can serve as a model for other successful platforms, such as GitHub, to adopt a similar approach in facilitating collaborative knowledge sharing. To showcase the practical applicability of our proposed framework, we demonstrate the development of a user interface concept that effectively addresses the complexities of collaborative knowledge sharing on Stack Overflow. This concept highlights the potential for Q\&A platforms to evolve into vibrant ecosystems that foster community-driven knowledge sharing. We further explore the feasibility of applying our framework to other successful platforms, such as GitHub, to facilitate collaborative knowledge sharing. To illustrate the applicability of our approach, we present a design concept for Stack Overflow's moderation dashboard, which demonstrates the effectiveness of bottom-up design and highlights the potential for Q\&A platforms to serve as dynamic knowledge-sharing environments.

Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's interests and level of knowledge.
To overcome the initial hurdle of discovering individuals' values and knowledge gaps,
our system will employ a dual role of participant classification and information recommendation.
Participants with similar values will be identified through clustering based on their
evaluation of climate-related statements, while their knowledge gaps will be estimated via
information retrieval analysis of their engagement level with relevant articles.
We anticipate our approach will motivate more people to become involved in climate discussions,
foster meaningful conversations, and encourage individuals to take action. 
Our method combines the techniques of participant classification and information retrieval to create
a personalized system, addressing the limitations of existing methods that rely on pre-defined categories
or prior knowledge of users' interests. 
This work will be presented at Knowledge Engineering with Answers.

Clinical symptom event extraction from unstructured doctor's notes is crucial for supervising medical treatments and analyzing patient outcomes. Although existing methods have achieved notable success in extracting events, their applicability is limited to specific datasets and institutions. This paper presents an innovative technique using self-supervised learning with unlabelled data to extract events with minimal adjustments needed, even in different settings. By applying this method to extracting symptoms and conditions from the Multi-Institutional Imperfect Mayo Clinic Pathology Dataset, we achieved impressive results, surpassing previous outcomes with a high degree of consistency across various sources. Furthermore, we observed that training on complete medical notes yields better results than training on just event-rich sections. Additionally, we found that using a hierarchical text prediction model increases accuracy in extracting less common events. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of self-supervised learning for event extraction and highlights best practices for achieving top results. All code and datasets are publicly available. In recent years, AI technologies based on neural networks have gained significant traction. However, the immense computational requirements for training and deployment have hindered widespread adoption, particularly in resource-constrained IoT applications. This hurdle has prompted the exploration of alternative models. Notably, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have emerged as a promising replacement, offering lower computational demands during training and inference. This study proposes a novel, resource-efficient deep learning framework based on SNNs, allowing for model training, compression, and accurate deployment on IoT devices. Our approach incorporates successive pruning during training, followed by sparsity-based compression, and yields a compact model requiring minimal memory. Our performance evaluations demonstrate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art compression techniques, and we illustrate the efficacy of this framework using simulations and real-world IoT sensor data. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Additionally, we investigated the effect of spin polarization and magnetic field on the mass of spin-polarized strange quark stars. Moreover, we studied the causal behavior of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field, and also, we investigated the effect of spin polarization, magnetic field, and temperature on the heat capacity and compressibility of spin-polarized strange quark matter. This analysis further led to the discovery of quantum oscillations in the density, energy density, pressure, heat capacity, compressibility, polarization, and magnetization of spin-polarized strange quark matter as a function of the 2nd component of the electron and quark Fermi momenta, which indicates the existence of 1st order phase transitions in the spin-polarized strange quark matter. Lastly, we studied the effect of spin polarization, magnetic field, and temperature on the transport properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter and obtained the relativistic transport equations for spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field, and also, we investigated the effect of spin polarization, magnetic field, and temperature on the dissipation of spin and magnetic fields in the spin-polarized strange quark matter. This analysis further led to the discovery of the relaxation time, in relation to the collisional relaxation time theory, for spin and magnetic fields in the spin-polarized strange quark matter as a function of the 2nd component of the electron and quark Fermi momenta. A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like image and video processing, and data compression. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated by demonstrating its deployment across diverse devices and environments, including desktop and mobile systems, and demonstrating its robustness through demonstrations of resilience in the face of faulty nodes within a volunteer computing pool. Finally, we investigated Pando's performance, finding that it excels on tasks that require a minimal number of computations but may struggle with more resource-intensive tasks due to an inherent limitation of performing computations on personal devices. Nonetheless, we are making Pando open-source, and invite contributions to help overcome these limitations and further advance the state-of-the-art in volunteer computing.

Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective in
solving a wide range of regression and classification problems, but their complex
predictions are difficult to interpret due to the inherent complexity of their
algorithm. To address this issue, a new method called Disentangled Attribution Curves
is proposed, which offers a more manageable way to understand the contributions of
each variable in enhancing model performance and correctly classifying instances. By
analyzing changes in the predicted target variable or classification outcome as
one variable is varied while others remain constant, the underlying structure of the
model can be revealed without the need for partial dependence plots or other complex
visualizations. This method is an interpretative tool that allows users to grasp the
models' behavior and identify potential areas of improvement. The effectiveness of
Disentangled Attribution Curves is demonstrated through experiments on benchmark
datasets using random forest and AdaBoost. The results show that this method can
significantly improve the interpretability of machine learning models by shedding
light on their strengths and weaknesses. Additionally, the findings suggest that
simple models can be developed that closely match the accuracy of more complex models
ensembles, such as random forest and AdaBoost. The proposed method is an
interpretative tool that allows users to understand the models' behavior and makes
model comparisons more straightforward, ultimately leading to the development of
more efficient and interpretable models that balance low bias and high variability. The
disentangled attribution curves can also be used as a diagnostic tool to assess
model performance and make adjustments as needed. Moreover, this method can be used
in various applications such as policy analysis, data visualization, and knowledge
extraction by providing insights into the models' behavior and outcomes. The future
directions of this research involve applying the method to real-world problems, as
well as exploring its potential uses in domains such as predictive analytics and
knowledge mining. To facilitate the use of this method, the associated code is
available on GitHub under the name DAC for random forests and AdaBoost. The method
can be used to compare the performance of different models, identify areas for

variability. The future directions of this research involve applying the method to

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local models, rather than sensitive data. However, if the parties' models are not securely developed, even seemingly private advancements can expose privacy breaches. Our proposed solution, tFLAST, offers a secure and private decentralized training method by utilizing Trusted Execution Environments and fast, efficient homomorphic processing of arithmetic operations on numbers. tFLAST establishes a secure protocol for trusted neural network development, relying on hardware-supported security and efficient aggregation of gradients through statistical testing for reliability. Our benchmarking results demonstrate that tFLAST can train models with accuracy equivalent to the standard Flast method, while significantly reducing training time by at least 10-20 times. Our system, designed for secure hardware support, can run in conjunction with standard software support, making public an open-source implementation of tFLAST to facilitate further research in its novel, hardware-assisted security features. The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing processes. To address these issues, this research presents a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. The proposed solution involves a device under test, a duplicating counterpart, and a central control unit. The control unit manages testing procedures while the device under test runs the code being tested and its counterpart simulates the interactions with external peripherals. The effectiveness of the solution was validated through various test protocols. The framework was applied to verify the code of a DC-motor driver, demonstrating its ability to find errors and ensure correct functionality of the code. The framework's efficiency was measured in terms of execution time and memory consumption. The proposed testing framework has been successfully implemented and demonstrated to effectively address the challenges of testing driver code. The evaluation showed that the framework is capable of detecting errors, providing accurate results, and operating within specified time and resource constraints. The framework offers a practical solution to the complex issue of testing driver code. The evaluation revealed an average error-detection rate of 95.5% and 97.5% for the DC-motor driver and the stepper-motor driver, respectively. The average error-detection rate was calculated based on the number of iterations required to detect all errors in the driver code. The proposed framework has potential applications in various industries, including automation and robotics. The framework offers a valuable tool for verifying the code of external-priority peripherals, providing a 100% error-detection rate in the tested protocols. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops, enabling short-term system call duration limits for microservices applications. It allows for precise limits to be imposed on system calls, preventing unapproved access to system resources. Timeloops analyzes historical system call durations to generate average patterns, then uses these patterns to determine allowed time periods for system calls. Microservices applications that fail to conform to these guidelines are blocked by Timeloops. As a rule-based system, Timeloops operates in real-time and does not disrupt the performance of applications. In contrast to static analysis-based techniques, Timeloops has a lightweight impact and is more suitable for modern, complex applications. Its efficacy was demonstrated in a test environment, where it effectively blocked malicious applications that target system vulnerabilities. In addition, Timeloops provides a detection mechanism for malicious applications that exploit system weaknesses. Its capabilities were shown to be effective in a test scenario involving a vulnerable e-commerce application. In terms of performance, Timeloops achieves low processing overheads of 1.4% to 6.9%, while maintaining accurate system call inspection rates of 99.9% to 100%. In terms of scalability, Timeloops supports up to 599 system calls per second, with an average processing latency of 0.42 milliseconds. Its lightweight design enables it to scale effectively, with the potential to support thousands of additional system calls per second. In conclusion, Timeloops offers a versatile and effective solution for short-term system call duration limits in microservices applications. Its innovative approach makes it a feasible option for replacing static analysis-based techniques, given its comparable or better performance at a lower cost. Future work may involve incorporating machine learning algorithms into Timeloops to further improve its accuracy in system call analysis. Additionally, Timeloops could be modified to include more sophisticated detection mechanisms for malicious applications, potentially utilizing other system metrics such as network traffic patterns. In the long run, Timeloops may be developed into an automated system for microservices security, with a human intervention step to define guidelines and a machine-driven component to enforce those guidelines. In this envisioned system, known as AEGIS, microservices developers would specify security requirements for their applications in a standardized format, while Timeloops would provide real-time system call limit enforcement. AEGIS would offer an automated system for detecting malicious applications, protecting system vulnerabilities, and blocking security threats. We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex spaces - and found that simpler methods excel here.
We can reduce the complexity of linear classification in complex spaces while maintaining performance, which has broader implications for the field.
This achievement enables the development of more efficient algorithms for matching tasks in the domain of product space embeddings.
As a result, we've created faster algorithms for producing consistent low-dimensional representations of data under varying geometric constraints.
We've also observed improvements in classification models and novel applications of product space embeddings in communities of nodes and clusters of associated data. 
This breakthrough has potential applications in advanced machine learning domains, including multi-aspect sentiment analysis and the detection of counterfeit products.

By utilizing the SPC (Star formation feedback powered by Planar gravitational Waves) model, researchers have developed a new simulation to study this phenomenon, resulting in a pattern consistent with observations of the Milky Way and other galaxies. Notably, the simulations reveal that stars are arranged in a bulging distribution at a distance of approximately 10 parsecs from the galactic center, aligning with break-up pattern observations. Furthermore, the models predict that the majority of stars within this galactic center region originated from two distinct galactic disks, specifically the younger inner disk and an older outer disk. Moreover, the models indicate that the break-up pattern is primarily shaped by the galactic center's peer-to-peer interactions, rather than its interactions with the surrounding disk, resulting in a break-up radius that is largely impervious to changes in supermassive black hole mass. Consequently, the models suggest that the break-up pattern can serve as a means to estimate the mass of the supermassive black hole without direct observation. In addition to the break-up pattern, the models reproduce several other well-documented break-up features, including an offset from the galactic center, a rotation in the opposite direction, and an uneven distribution among the stars. In various learning tasks like signal processing and computer vision, exploiting sparsity and structure in data can significantly aid in reducing computational demands by taking advantage of inherent properties present in the data. Compressive learning is an emerging field that incorporates sparsity and structure from the beginning by formulating problems in a compressed form. However, existing methods in compressive learning still assume complete knowledge of the system, which is often not the case in real-world scenarios. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a new approach based on Bayesian inference that allows for learning the system and signal sparsity patterns simultaneously from compressed measurements. We utilize a Gaussian process model to capture the complex system behavior and a sparse Gaussian prior to represent the signal, leveraging the GP's properties such as nonparametricity and flexibility. We develop an approximate inference method grounded in variational Bayesian and expectation propagation to enable scalable learning from compressed data. Our approach is evaluated on a range of simulations that demonstrate its effectiveness in extracting the system and signal patterns from compressed measurements, surpassing traditional compressive learning methods. Our method is further applied to an image recovery problem, where the results show its capability in reconstructing the images and extracting the underlying sparse patterns from the compressed images. Although accuracy levels are acceptable for practical purposes, this approach has potential for improving timekeeping accuracy on satellites, in addition to providing benefits in various fields such as orientation and camera calibration. Finally, leveraging this information, researchers can develop a novel application oriented towards educational and general audiences, enabling the determination of time and day from a single minimum set of camera phone measurements. This application has various potential uses, including educational settings where it can facilitate learning about astronomy and mathematics, as well as provide useful information for everyday purposes. This study's findings serve as a basis for further research in several areas, with potential for collaboration in multiple fields. To demonstrate the study's efficacy, a working prototype implementation is presented, showcasing its potential in everyday scenarios. The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of sentence $\Phi'$ are all bipartite graph representations.  Consequently, we deduce that, in order to resolve Asser's conjecture regarding the class's closure under complement, we may focus solely on examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs.  Finally, we introduce a collection of sentences, denoted as $\mathcal{C}$, with at most three variables and one binary relation, demonstrating that any such sentence, $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, $\Phi'$, also using at most three variables and one binary relation, whose model cardinalities increase linearly, whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs, and whose models are all 2-embeddable into the models of $\Phi$.  We also deduce that, in order to resolve Adeleke and Ghannad's conjecture regarding the class's closure under homomorphism, we may focus solely on examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs and are 2-embeddable into the models of another given sentence, $\Phi$.  We also introduce a family of finite structures, $T_n$, each consisting of undirected bipartite graphs with at most three variables, whose number of elements increase polynomially, and whose $k$-homomorphism density tends to zero for any given integer $k$.  We also partially resolve Adeleke and Ghannad's conjecture regarding the class's closure under homomorphism by demonstrating that, in the limit of a specific class of finite structures, the $k$-homomorphism density of any given sentence, $\Phi$, either always exceeds zero or never exceeds zero, and if it never exceeds zero, then its complement's $k$-homomorphism density always exceeds zero.  We achieve this by utilizing a modified version of the Bruck-Kahane-Sjöstrand theorem. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Additionally, the thermal capacity exhibits a sublinear temperature dependence due to constraints imposed by chiral symmetry, in addition to a temperature-independent term that is a dimensionless function of the coupling strength. By contrast, the compressibility shows a more intricate temperature behavior that differs significantly from the expectations of Fermi liquid theory. These results can be attributed to the unique characteristics of Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which lead to correlations exhibiting distinct scaling behaviors at large and small distances from one another. These findings are also interpreted in terms of the manifestations of Kondo binding and the formation of a bound state at low temperatures, giving rise to a picture of thermal screening through Kondo binding that occurs throughout the entire material. This material is of particular interest due to recent experimental measurements of thermal capacity and compressibility in relation to graphene's density. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. Masked Speech Synthesis is an effective approach for improving sequence-to-sequence models' performance by incorporating additional masking strategies. However, a systematic investigation of the effect of masking schemes on contextual modeling has yet to be conducted. Furthermore, a thorough examination of the impact of masking quantities on contextual modeling has not been explored. To address these gaps, we undertake an exhaustive analysis of eight masking schemes across various contextual masking quantities to establish a baseline for contextual modeling. Our research assesses the quality of novel views using Mean Opinion Score and acoustic metrics while analyzing the relationship between contextual masking schemes and their performance. These findings lead to the development of an optimized masking strategy, enabling the enhancement of contextual modeling capabilities and subsequently producing superior paragraph-level speech synthesis. Our model produces paragraph-level speech with significantly lower word error rates and higher speech quality, outperforming the vanilla Transformer by 0.15 WER and 0.07 MOS. Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Our proposed approach, Deep Stealing, manifests as a non-query attack where the attacker intercepts data, applies transformations, and returns the modified data to the victim, without requiring knowledge of the model parameters. Our experiments on standard datasets, specifically CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, showcase the success of this method against DNN models, including both supervised and semi-supervised classifications. Additionally, our analysis on Deep Stealing's characteristics and implications highlights its significant adverse impacts, including compromised accuracy, security breaches, and potential financial losses. Our research also delves into potential mitigation strategies, specifically the deployment of Clean Data policies, to prevent such attacks and maintain model integrity. This research represents a pioneering effort in understanding the vulnerability of DNN models to MitM attacks and initiating a new line of inquiry in security research. Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies. This study utilizes a novel software tool for automatically detecting stances in social media posts, allowing researchers to conduct such analyses more efficiently. Existing tools often require manual data labeling or have limited capabilities, making our tool a valuable resource for researchers to conduct similar studies. 

Key findings:
1. Social media platforms like Twitter serve as significant channels for disseminating conspiracy theories regarding climate change, constituting approximately 11% of all climate change-related conversations.
2. Conspiracy theories are often presented as personal opinions rather than verified facts, underscoring their sophisticated nature.
3. Non-climate change believers predominantly share tweets related to conspiracy theories.
4. Believers in human-caused climate change tend to share conspiracy theories that attribute the issue to human activities, such as population growth, resource consumption, and industrial activities, thereby aligning their stances.
5. Social media users who are skeptical of climate change but not conspiracy theory believers, on the other hand, disseminate a broader range of conspiracy theories that also include those attributing the issue to human activities and environmental factors.

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of various particles such as protons, neutrons, and electrons to achieve this goal, creating and using anti-matter particles is particularly challenging due to their tendency to combine with their opposite counterparts.
Specific challenges arise from producing and identifying specific anti-matter particles, particularly light ones such as antineutrinos, which can decay into electrons capable of being easily detected but were undetected in previous experiments.
A proposed experimental setup, called AMANAI, aims to overcome these obstacles by using a unique beam of muons with low momentum to target anti-matter particles produced in the $^6$Li$^\ast$ when hit by high-energy gamma-rays produced through nuclear reactions.
Given the novel setup and its challenges, an optimization study of the experiment's capabilities to identify antineutrinos decaying into electrons is presented, taking into consideration various physical decays and their observability.
Results show that the detection of a specific type of antineutrino decay into electrons may be feasible with a data sample of $10^9$ incident muon decays, which can be obtained within a time frame of a few years with the described experimental configuration.
A discussion on how to identify other produced anti-matter particles, such as antiprotons and antineutrons, in conjunction with electrons from various sources is also provided, along with potential future improvements for the experiment. 
These improvements could involve supplementing the experiment with an external magnetic field to enhance the detection of a wide range of exotic particles, and incorporating a new fast and highly efficient neutron detector to verify the production of antineutrons.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic structures. These changes lead to two distinct phases of evolution: stabilization and further evolution. We analyzed real-time data from the JUNO radio telescope and found a noise storm associated with a microflare that exhibited both phases. During the first phase, the base frequency of the storm source decreased by about 0.2 MHz/min, while its bandwidth increased at a rate of approximately 0.3 MHz/min. This was followed by a steady increase in the base frequency of about 0.1 MHz/minute, along with a bandwidth that leveled off at around 5 MHz. We observed the base frequency of the storm source continue to rise over a period of about 270 minutes, although its amplitude remained relatively consistent. We considered various factors that may influence the storm source, including changes in the beam density, the size of the beam, and the distribution of radio frequency spectral index, but were unable to determine a consistent change in any of these parameters. Therefore, we were unable to provide a fully theoretical explanation for the observed behavior of the storm source. Nonetheless, our study of the storm source reveals that its evolution is more complex than initially anticipated, and further research is needed to understand the dynamics of noise storms. The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied at the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror. Moreover, our study investigates total scattering lengths for scalar and vector interactions, comparing these lengths when the atom and mirror have opposite charges to the scenario in which they have the same charge. These investigations of scattering processes provide crucial insights into the physical phenomena occurring at the atom-mirror interface. For all evaluations, our results are normalized to the case where the atom and mirror are at rest and have the same properties. These findings are further generalized to the case of relativistic atoms, providing essential theoretical agreements with established perspectives. These analyses ultimately yield expressions for photon emission rates when an excited atom undergoes constant acceleration, deceleration, or cyclic motion, as well as scenarios involving radial or random motion. To validate our model's validity, we present tangible spontaneous emission rates calculated for specific cases of an initially excited hydrogen-like ion either accelerating or decelerating. These calculations demonstrate a significant variation in spontaneous emission rates, ranging from a reduction of over two orders in magnitude to an increase of the same order. Additionally, we show that the highest spontaneous emission rates are observed when an excited atom decelerates or an excited ion accelerates. Based on these findings, we suggest that an atom or ion experiences the most significant changes in spontaneous emission rates when it experiences deceleration. These theoretical predictions are compared with the most advanced computational methods available today, including the relativistic quantum electrodynamical approaches. Our study also discusses the broad applicability of our model in theoretical physics, highlighting its potential application to the investigation of novel optical phenomena occurring at the atom-mirror interface, including the likely generation of entangled photon states through either constant or variable motion. Furthermore, the outcomes of our model can be utilized to develop innovative strategies for the controlled generation of entangled photons, exemplified by the feasible creation of entangled photons through the deceleration of an excited hydrogen-like ion. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they can be considered true outliers or if their natal locations were simply obscured by early interactions with nearby clusters.  Recent discoveries of massive stars in "field" populations have been particularly significant as they suggest these stars formed outside of dense clusters, however these findings have also been countered by suggestions that these locations were actually obscured by early interactions with nearby clusters, a phenomenon known as "confinement".  To help address this question, a search was conducted for massive stars in the Westerlund 2 rich cluster and its surrounding fields using a novel approach of analyzing the spatial distribution of both the clusters and stars.  This analysis revealed that the cluster was surrounded by a larger, halo-like structure that extended at least 20 degrees in space, and also discovered a significant number of runaway stars located near the cluster's edge and in its surrounding fields.  These findings suggested that the cluster and its surrounding fields were linked through dynamic interactions and star-formation processes, and also indicated that many of the cluster's stars originated from outside of the cluster itself.  This research has important implications for understanding how massive stars are formed, particularly in the context of the "massive star problem" which seeks to explain how massive stars are formed efficiently despite requiring large amounts of gas to form a star".  This research also provides new insights into the origins of the rich cluster, Westerlund 2, and its surrounding fields, and also contributes to our understanding of the broader field of star clusters and their development.  This research used data from the VVV survey, an infrared star cluster survey that originated in 2010 and is one of the richest collections of star clusters in the Milky Way.  This research also utilized the VISTA telescope, which is one of the VVV's key observational tools, and is located at the ESO Paranal Observatory in the Chilean Atacama Desert. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. However, these approaches run the risk of overfitting when applied to sparse institutional data. To counteract this limitation, this paper proposes an innovative deep learning-based method for channel estimation in institutional settings. The suggested approach utilizes a long short-term memory (LSTM) unit to tap into the temporal dependencies within the IEEE 802.11p signal, thereby enhancing channel estimation accuracy using fewer pilot symbols. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method surpasses currently available DL-based and conventional estimators in institutional settings, also requiring fewer pilot symbols for optimal results. Additionally, the proposed solution demonstrates adaptability across different operational environments, requiring only minor adjustments to match new scenarios. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another complication arises from training neural networks, which typically requires paired images containing corresponding color information. Since obtaining large datasets of accurately colored images can be a significant undertaking, researchers have explored alternative approaches involving single-image colorization using pre-trained models. These models leverage image attributes and learn to generate colors by predicting them, effectively transforming the task into supervised learning. This paper delves into the latest developments in single-image colorization, including the principles behind existing methods and their comparisons. Furthermore, it presents a novel approach called Photo2Paint, which utilizes an image transformer and a conditional Gaussian Mixture Model to determine color likelihoods. The proposed method outperforms existing methods in maintaining local consistency while generating richer, more detailed colors. Assessment of the model's performance reveals its superiority over the current state of the art, as evident from the provided examples and supplementary material. A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.  A specific case study highlights the practical utility of this estimator in bias reduction.  Note that while this proposal is rooted in a traditional framework, it may struggle with issues of consistency in the presence of irregularity.  This proposal can, however, serve as a foundation for further development in both bias reduction and high-dimensional contexts. when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task

accuracy and F1 scores across diverse datasets, including those of biomedical and
general nature. Furthermore, our findings indicated that models' abilities to
predict links between subjects and objects can serve as indicators of their
performance in traditional relation extraction tasks. As such, we recommend the

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm. We provide concrete examples illustrating our findings and their implications. Ultimately, our study contributes to understanding how the prime factorization of $d$ influences the behavior of lattice minima and the algorithmic computation of the principal factorization type of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$. Our work complements previous research by Baker and Davenport on the number field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ and its extension by the 3rd primitive cube root of unity $\zeta_3$. Moreover, our findings have applications to number fields generally, not just those of degree $3$. Our work also examines the behavior of the lattice minima in the quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ and their relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals in the context of the prime factorization of $d$. As such, our study is relevant to the broader field of algebraic number theory. Our analysis is further reinforced by numerous accompanying images and graphs that illustrate our findings. To date, these images are the first of their kind in this field of study. In addition, our code for computing the lattice minima and their associated generators is included as an appendix. Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have uncovered fascinating binary formation processes in massive star clusters. Specifically, observations of six core masses ($< 0.1 M_{\odot}$) have demonstrated the binary formation process in five of these cores by detecting binary fragments. The mass of these fragments ranges from $0.1 M_{\odot}$ to $2 M_{\odot}$. A significant finding is that cores with lower total mass had higher fragment masses. Among the cores with similar fragment masses, those with lower total mass were observed to have lighter binary masses. Using theoretical models, it was determined to what extent binary formation could occur within these cores by simulating two-ninth mass fractions. The results indicate that cores with lower total mass are more likely to produce binary systems and that lighter binary masses are preferred in these systems. The observed tendency of lower total mass leading to higher fragment masses is also replicated in the theoretical models. However, the theoretical models fail to replicate the observed heavier binary masses in two of the cores, which could be attributed to the influence of supersonic turbulence on binary formation. Further study is required to understand binary formation in such systems. The new discoveries present an exciting opportunity to study stellar formation through high-resolution radio observations of massive star clusters. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick can circumvent assumptions of linearity in ICA, most existing methods involve complex nonlinear functions that make the algorithm slow. We have developed a novel, efficient algorithm for estimating the transformed matrix 'W' and an optimization procedure for tuning the kernel's parameters in'm-ar-K-FastICA'. When comparing our approach to other state-of-the-art methods, such as kPCA and kernel independent component analysis, we found that it outperforms them in terms of speed and accuracy. Additionally, we found that'm-ar-K-FastICA' performs better than FastICA and its derivatives in a simulated artificial dataset. We have also validated our approach using the EEGLAB tool on real EEG signals from subjects engaged in various cognitive tasks. Our results show that'm-ar-K-FastICA' successfully extracts the most relevant features from brain activity while minimizing computation time. With its superior efficiency and accuracy, our approach is now readily available through the EEGLAB tool for feature extraction in scientific research. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and social structure factors are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, decision trees consistently outperformed other models across multiple evaluations. Moreover, our research found that rumors are primarily propagated through social media platforms, as well as a significant correlation between a rumor's popularity and the public's anxiety level. Ultimately, our study provides insights for understanding the spread of online rumors in China during the early pandemic. In light of our methodology's versatility, our analysis may be adapted to study rumor dynamics in diverse contexts. Additionally, our framework can be utilized by policymakers to make data-driven decisions regarding public health campaigns aimed at mitigating the impact of online rumors. Based on this backdrop, there is a growing need to create more interpretable models that can still deliver strong performance. This goal can be achieved by utilizing a subset of the neural network's parameters, often referred to as 'lottery tickets,' which can be trained independently and simultaneously provide strong performance and interpretability. This paper aims to understand the underlying patterns within these subsets, identifying common characteristics and any variations that may exist, and presents a comprehensive analysis of the common characteristics within these subsets, including their distribution, layer variation, and functional properties. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that 'lottery tickets' can be utilized to create data representations that are both interpretable and useful, and also shows that these representations can be used to develop models with strong generalization capabilities capable of detecting relevant features within the data. This study employs a comprehensive approach, utilizing numerical simulations and experimental evidence, to investigate the effects of various loss functions on deep neural network training and classification accuracy. Our results indicate that the optimal loss function is highly dependent on the dataset and algorithmic setup, whereas a related finding shows that the order of data points presented during training can also impact model performance. Furthermore, by analyzing the distribution of model parameters across different loss functions, our study reveals that a loss function's optimal model is often characterized by extreme deviations in parameter values compared to the dataset's mean, thereby providing insights into the deep learning dynamics. These findings shed new light on the deep learning process, highlighting the significance of data presentation order, and demonstrate the potential of loss functions to effectively control the generalization performance of neural networks. Additionally, our study provides a comprehensive review of recent research on the effects of data presentation order on the dynamics of neural networks. Based on these findings, we propose an intuitive, yet effective, method for optimizing loss functions by leveraging the distribution of model parameters. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, when compared to the original original method. A key system parameter is the frequency at which safety community members receive follow-up messages (responses) from specialists. Specialists' ability to encourage (persuade) community members to provide additional information is a key strategy for enhancing system performance, particularly response rates, which is a major system goal. A key question arises as to what impact specialists' emotional support (encouragement) has on community members' engagement in these systems. This study addressed this query by analyzing data from a system comprising over 18,000 users and indicating a statistically significant correlation between specialists' emotional support and users' response rates. Notably, users who received emotional support from specialists showed a 25% increased response rate compared to those who did not receive such support. Further analysis revealed that specialists' emotional support had a more significant effect on community members who had previously gone silent (ceased interacting with the system), persuading about 30% more responses from these individuals. This study's findings have significant system-level and user-level implications, suggesting the potential for specialists to effectively use emotional support to enhance system performance, particularly response rates, by influencing user behavior and potentially reversing system dropout. A key strategy for specialists to enhance system performance involves combining (a) pressure on unresponsive users (to maintain system performance) with (b) emotional support to encourage user engagement (to enhance system performance), particularly from previously unresponsive community members. This study's findings open the door for system administrators to explore these possibilities in their systems. A key limitation of this study is the potential for specialists to provide emotional support based on their personal opinions rather than system-encouraged behavior, which may introduce bias in the study's findings. Therefore, recommending system-encouraged responses moderated by specialists' personal opinions could yield more accurate results in these scenarios. This study demonstrates the potential for researchers to investigate other previously unexplored factors in text-based systems, particularly those influencing user behavior and system performance, such as system administrators, including system response rates. A key strategy for system administrators to enhance system performance involves identifying and responding to potentially abusive messages from specialists, which may have a more significant effect on system performance, particularly response rates, than specialist emotional support. These classifiers are trained on different subsets of labeled data, sourced from various human annotators. This approach leverages diversity in human opinions to produce robust ensemble predictions and effectively generalizes to missing data. The proposed method performs competitively on hard instances and achieves superior results in semi-supervised learning tasks compared to traditional active learning techniques. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions in a condensed visualization of the parameter space, indicating areas where comparisons deviate from expected results. By doing so, we can efficiently extract valuable information, reduce labeling costs by approximately one order of magnitude, and achieve optimal results without necessitating a thorough model re-training. Our method has been successfully applied to enhance the performance of models for generating summaries, answering questions, and identifying objects, in multiple tasks. Notably, it has even surpassed the performance achieved through more extensive comparative evaluations, both in samples of synthetic data and in real-world scenarios involving language translation and image classification. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which are often overlooked in single-study analyses. In our comprehensive comparison of 16 datasets across 7 domains, consistent differences in performance between model calibration and density estimation were observed across background and semantic shifts, highlighting their limitations in adaptating to changing data characteristics. These findings raise questions about the feasibility of developing a universal method for identifying out-of-distribution examples and the potential benefits of designing datasets that encourage more efficient learning of concept drifts. Our study provides a reference point for future research on this topic.

A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of elements, we can define a more intricate operation, known as the f-Convolution, which can be computed efficiently using a brute-force approach in $O(|D|^2)$ time when one function is a constant, where $|D|$ represents the size of domain $D$. Further investigations into the properties of $\oplus_f$ and f-Convolution are conducted, and several pressing questions regarding their underlying non-deterministic polynomial time hardness are explored. Finally, the fundamental differences between the convolution types, specifically the behavior of $\oplus_f$ and $\otimes_f$, are analyzed and their variations in complexity are understood, and a general framework for determining the computational complexity of convolution is presented, and their results are formally stated and proven. This study utilizes the NOIRLAIMedians3d code to perform a thorough atmospheric reconstruction of GJ 229B's spectrum, utilizing simultaneous optical and near-infrared data collected by the La Silla 3.6-meter telescope in 1995. The reconstruction indicates that the companion has a mass of 49 to 79 solar masses and temperatures of 750-900 K. The analysis also detects sub-weak-line methane absorption for the first time in a substellar object, which may be attributed to the presence of larger than typical methane and water droplets in the atmosphere of GJ 229B, given the lack of data on similar objects and late-type T-dwarfs. The study further examines the atmospheric parameters of GJ 229B, including the estimate of its gravitational log g strength, which may be subject to significant uncertainty due to the assumptions of hydrostatic equilibrium. The analysis of the spectrum within the framework of the proxy technique yields ages estimates of 0.2-0.5 Gy for the GJ 229 system, which is consistent with other young moving groups such as the AB Dor and T-association Watne groups. The presence of a T-dwarf like GJ 229B in the USNO-A2.0 catalog is unlikely due to the detection efficiency of current and future surveys. The comparison of the atmospheric features of late-type T-dwarfs and extremely low-mass brown dwarfs, which is to be conducted with the help of future observations and the upcoming SPHERE, should ultimately reveal whether late-type T-dwarfs and extremely low-mass brown dwarfs belong to distinct categories or are part of a continuous spectrum of objects in the mass-temperature diagram. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. To achieve this, we created an matching algorithm and implemented it using long-lived actors on top of the Akka framework. Our approach combines the actor model with the matching algorithm to provide efficient handling of incoming requests from multiple sources. To evaluate our system, we conducted benchmark testing on a computer with an Intel Core i5 processor and 8 GB of RAM, using a score-aware double-sided auction to analyze its performance under various scenarios. To summarize, our double-sided auctions are designed to support multiple quantity trade requests, have a scalable architecture, and provide efficient matching services. In modern research on data-driven systems, a major focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional nonparametric and parametric models, as well as delayed dynamical systems. The lack of robust statistical tools to support these models limits their practical applications. This work aims to address this gap by developing an innovative integrated framework, which utilizes combined Bayesian posterior convergence and intrinsic convergence to ensure accurate learning from delayed data in high-dimensional nonparametric models. The framework's effectiveness is empirically demonstrated across multiple real-world case studies in multi-step forecasting, where the incorporation of temporal constraints helps to mitigate the effects of delay and achieve superior forecasting outcomes compared to traditional delayed dynamical models. The proposed framework thus offers a practical solution for addressing delayed data in real-world applications. Furthermore, the study provides a theoretical understanding of delayed data through the lens of nonparametric regression theory, highlighting the significance of posterior integration and temporal consistency in delaying observations. Importantly, the results remain universally applicable to any statistical model, beyond delayed dynamical systems alone. Lastly, the study explores the properties of delayed data, identifying key characteristics and challenges that complicate learning from delayed data, particularly in high-dimensional settings. The investigation shows that delaying observations tends to distort their distribution, along with introducing challenges of partial confounding and feedback effects that complicate the learning process. Hence, the proposed approach offers a valuable contribution to the literature, facilitating the development of accurate delay-adjusted forecasting of delayed data in real-world applications. Once these subtasks are identified, the external reward system becomes sufficient, allowing the intrinsic drives to be disabled. Our results are validated through an analysis of the learned policies and the dynamics of both the intrinsic and external drives during the learning process. Ultimately, the incorporation of end-effect drives presents an efficient solution for inverting a target distribution, especially in scenarios with scarce external reward signals. Our method is applicable to a range of real-world tasks, such as Kung Fu Swing robotic arm manipulation and the Inverted Pole balancing task. A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory. Our work has also revealed that specific model parameters may yield simplified descriptions, particularly in the context of the Minkowski space limit, in accordance with the standard Poincaré algebra. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the diversity of particle models that arise from our algebraic framework, which contrasts with the conventional approaches used to describe particles with spin in three dimensions.
